title: Interés menguante, desconfianza y polarización: Así se informan los españoles
content:
Los españoles están llamados a votar en las elecciones generales de este domingo. Los sondeos sugieren que Pedro Sánchez, que ha gobernado el país desde 2018, podría perder el poder. Las elecciones son un buen momento para explorar cómo los españoles se informan con la ayuda de más de una década de datos del Digital News Report.

Nuestros datos muestran que las audiencias más jóvenes tienen menos confianza y menos interés en las noticias, y son las más propensas a usar chatbots y redes sociales para informarse. La confianza en la radiotelevisión pública divide profundamente a los españoles, la preocupación por la desinformación en línea está en su punto más alto y muchos critican la cobertura que los medios hacen del clima y la inmigración. A continuación, presentamos nueve hallazgos de nuestro informe.

title: Shrinking interest and divided trust: How Spaniards get their news
content:
Spaniards will soon head to the polls for a snap general election on 29 November. The latest polls suggest the vote is an uphill battle for the country’s centre-left prime minister. After being in power since 2018, Pedro Sánchez now risks being ousted by a right-wing government. The election is a good moment to explore how Spaniards get their news with the help of more than a decade of survey data from our Digital News Report. 

Our surveys show news use in Spain is divided across age groups, with younger audiences more critical, less interested and more likely to use AI chatbots and social media for news than older age groups. Both interest and trust have plummeted in the past decade, with trust in the public broadcaster deeply polarised along political lines. Many Spaniards are critical of climate and immigration coverage, and concerns about online misinformation are at their peak. Here are nine findings from our research.

title: Interested but not Engaged: How Europe's Media Cover Brexit
content:
What do the media of other EU member countries consider to be important as the UK negotiates being the first country to leave the EU? How much and what kind of national self-interest does the Brexit decision trigger? What do European media think about Brexit and the UK’s way of dealing with it? These are some of the questions that Alexandra Borchardt, Felix M. Simon and Diego Bironzo answer in this Reuters Institute and Prime Research report.

Brexit is less than 300 days away and, perhaps unsurprisingly, European media take great interest in the fate of the United Kingdom and the current state of the negotiations between the country and the EU. Yet, despite the UK’s departure into the unknown, Europe’s media appear mostly unconcerned about the UK leaving the bloc. Instead, the newest report by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism shows a European press which is attentive to but not agitated by Brexit. While the coverage is shaped by national perspectives, the overriding impression is that of a largely homogenous and objective attitude towards one of the most important developments in recent European history.

title: New platforms and shrinking trust: How Brazilians get their news
content:
Brazilians will soon head to the polls for the second round of their presidential election. The vote is a close contest between left-wing incumbent Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro. The election is a good moment to explore how Brazilians get their news, how much they trust it and what are their attitudes towards it. Here are seven findings based on more than a decade of survey data from our Digital News Report. 

Social media surpassed TV as the most widely used source of news in Brazil during the pandemic. But its use for news has declined 19 points in the past decade along with almost every news source.

  • The only ascendant news source is AI chatbots, whose use for news is growing fast, especially within the youngest age groups. One in five (19%) Brazilians under 25 say they use AI chatbots for news.
